Empirical Research Plan –  “Price-Sensitivity of Health‐Insurance Take-Up Among the Self-Employed After TRA86”

────────────────────────────────────────
1. Identification Strategy
────────────────────────────────────────
Method:  Difference-in-Differences (DID) implemented in a 2-stage-least-squares framework (DID-IV).

• Reduced form (DID):  Estimate the causal impact of TRA86 on the probability that a self-employed person is insured, using wage-and-salary workers as a control group and pre- vs. post-TRA86 years for timing.

• Structural interpretation (DID-IV):  Translate the policy effect into a price elasticity by instrumenting the individual’s after-tax price of insurance (a continuous endogenous regressor) with the exogenous interaction
 Zit  = SelfEmpi × Postt .
This delivers the Local Average Treatment Effect of a 1-percent change in after-tax price on the extensive-margin insurance decision.

Why appropriate?
– The reform generated a large, sudden, and group-specific shock to the after-tax price that is plausibly exogenous to individual health-coverage trends.  
– DID eliminates common macro shocks; IV eliminates endogeneity of price arising from plan choice and health risk.

────────────────────────────────────────
2. Treatment and Control
────────────────────────────────────────
Treatment variable (endogenous regressor):  
 Priceit  =  after-tax premium / face premium  
(constructed with TAXSIM, tax rules, and a national premium schedule).

Instrument (treatment assignment):  
 Zit  =  SelfEmpi × Postt  

Definitions
• SelfEmpi = 1 if individual earned ≥$2,000 self-employment income and < $2,000 wage-salary income in calendar year.  
• Postt = 1 for insurance status reported for tax years 1988–89 (observed in March 1989 & 1990 CPS).  
• Control group:  wage-and-salary workers (SelfEmp=0) aged 25–54.  
• Pre-period: 1985–86 (March 86 & 87 CPS).  
• Event date: Tax Reform Act of 1986 (effective for 1987 tax year; we omit 1987 transition year).

Supplementary specifications use a triple-difference that further interacts Zit with the individual’s statutory marginal tax rate to exploit heterogeneity in the size of the price shock.

────────────────────────────────────────
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
────────────────────────────────────────
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of TRA86, self-employed and wage workers would have exhibited similar trends in insurance coverage.  
 Plausibility: Pre-reform CPS years (e.g., 1981–86) show roughly parallel movements; no contemporaneous reforms targeted only the self-employed.

A2. No differential compositional change: TRA86 did not differentially alter who becomes self-employed in ways correlated with unobserved insurance tastes.  
 Plausibility: Self-employment entry rates are stable in CPS; we will control for observable covariates and check balance.

A3. Exclusion restriction for IV:  The interaction SelfEmp × Post affects insurance coverage only through its impact on the after-tax price, not through other channels (e.g., income shocks).  
 Plausibility: Wage workers faced similar rate cuts; the only policy difference for the self-employed was the new 25 % deduction for premiums.

A4. Stable Unit Treatment Value (no spillovers): One person’s treatment does not affect another’s decision in a way that differs by employment type.  
 Plausibility: Individual health-insurance decisions are largely independent across groups.

────────────────────────────────────────
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation
────────────────────────────────────────
T1. Non-parallel pre-trends.  
 • Check: Visual and formal event-study using 1981–86 CPS waves.  
 • Fix:  Include individual controls (age, sex, education, state × year FE) and weight observations; drop industries with structural shocks.

T2. Concurrent TRA86 provisions (marginal-rate cuts) change labor supply or income differently for the self-employed.  
 • Check:  Test for differential changes in hours, earnings, self-employment entry.  
 • Fix:  Triple-difference by statutory marginal tax bracket; include earnings controls; restrict to continuous self-employed.

T3. Measurement error in constructed prices (due to imputed premiums).  
 • Check:  Validate against SIPP self-reported premiums.  
 • Fix:  Use IV which is robust to classical measurement error; perform robustness with alternative premium schedules (e.g., by age-gender cell).

────────────────────────────────────────
5. R Code Outline
────────────────────────────────────────
```r
# -------------------------------------------
# 0.  Packages
# -------------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)       # fast DID / IV regressions
library(modelsummary) # neat tables

# -------------------------------------------
# 1.  Load & combine CPS files (CSV)
# -------------------------------------------
years <- c(1986, 1987, 1989, 1990)   # March files
cps_list <- lapply(years, function(y){
  fread(paste0("cps_march_", y, ".csv"))[, survey_year := y]
})
cps <- rbindlist(cps_list, fill = TRUE)

# -------------------------------------------
# 2.  Sample restrictions
# -------------------------------------------
cps <- cps[
  age >= 25 & age <= 54 &
  !is.na(hins_priv)                 # private HI coverage indicator
]

# -------------------------------------------
# 3.  Key variables
# -------------------------------------------
cps[, selfemp := as.integer(se_inc >= 2000 & ws_inc < 2000)]
cps[, post    := as.integer(survey_year %in% c(1989, 1990))]     # covers 1988–89 status
cps[, treat   := selfemp * post]

# After-tax price (constructed previously via TAXSIM; assume var = at_price)
# Standardize: price as log of after-tax premium relative to face value
cps[, lprice := log(at_price)]

# Covariates
covars <- c("age", "I(age^2)", "female", "married", "black", "hisp",
            "educ_college", "exper", "exper_sq",
            "statefip", "industry", "occupation")

# -------------------------------------------
# 4.  First stage (DID)
# -------------------------------------------
fs_formula <- as.formula(
  paste("lprice ~ treat |",                 # endogenous ~ instrument
        "statefip + survey_year +",         # fixed effects
        paste(covars, collapse = " + "))
)

first_stage <- feols(
  fs_formula,
  iv = ~ 1 | treat,
  data = cps,
  weights = ~ person_weight               # CPS weight
)

# -------------------------------------------
# 5.  Second stage (2SLS DID)
# -------------------------------------------
ss_formula <- as.formula(
  paste("hins_priv ~ lprice | treat |",    # outcome ~ endogenous | instrument
        "statefip + survey_year +",
        paste(covars, collapse = " + "))
)

second_stage <- feols(
  ss_formula,
  iv = ~ lprice | treat,
  data = cps,
  weights = ~ person_weight,
  cluster = ~ statefip                     # cluster by state
)

modelsummary(list("First Stage" = first_stage,
                  "Second Stage" = second_stage),
             gof_omit = "Adj")

# -------------------------------------------
# 6.  Robustness check – event study
# -------------------------------------------
cps[, rel_time := (survey_year - 1986)]    # 0 = last pre year
for(t in -3:3) cps[, paste0("D",t) := as.integer(rel_time == t & selfemp==1)]

event_form <- paste("hins_priv ~", 
                    paste(paste0("D", -3:3)[-4], collapse = " + "), "|",   # omit D0
                    "statefip + survey_year +", paste(covars, collapse = " + "))

event_est <- feols(as.formula(event_form),
                   data = cps, cluster = ~ statefip)

```

────────────────────────────────────────
6. Expected Results
────────────────────────────────────────
Theory predicts a negative elasticity: lowering the after-tax price raises the probability of buying insurance.

Prior studies of employer mandates find extensive-margin elasticities between −0.4 and −0.8.  
Because self-employed face the full premium price, I expect a somewhat larger sensitivity:  
 ε ≈ −1.0 (i.e., a 10 % fall in the after-tax price raises coverage by ~10 percentage points from a base of ~45 %).

────────────────────────────────────────
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment
────────────────────────────────────────
DID / IV Checklist (1 = satisfied, 0 = questionable)

C1  Parallel pre-trends visually absent ………………… 1  
C2  No differential compositional change ………………. 0.8  
C3  No simultaneous policy confounds …………………… 0.7  
C4  Strong first-stage (F > 10) ……………………………… 1  
C5  Exclusion restriction (only price channel) ………… 0.7  

Overall: The design is credible, but residual concern remains about other TRA86 effects on the self-employed; robustness checks and triple-difference mitigate—yet cannot fully eliminate—this worry.

────────────────────────────────────────
